answer: A market can make reputation costly to multiply: each agent must lock a scarce, nontransferable stake as an anchor before it can trade, and lose part of it when peers prove fraud under a defined dispute rule. The stake does not prove a unique human, but it makes a swarm of fresh identities expensive: each needs its own capital, while splitting one stake across a vine of accounts risks detection and forfeiture. A trellis of shared transaction histories lets buyers weigh proven behavior, not names alone.
